blocks.html: It is a maxim spread through all the parts of the law, That more faith must be given to two witnesses who assure and affirm something than to six hundred or to a thousand who deny a; inasmuch as, as the Philosopher says, he knows better, and with greater certainty, who understands the thing in question by affirmation and assurance, than he who knows it by denial b. For also, by the nature of things, it is almost impossible to prove a negation: for how could it be proved that Antoine had never been at Toulouse? Contrariwise, therefore, where the difficulty of proof would not arise, this rule too would have no place d. Example: in a college of a university, to examine a scholar and approve him for the degree of Doctorate, seven doctors at the least are necessary e; of whom, if three assure his sufficiency and approve him, and the four others deny it and reject him, the testimony of these latter, as being the greater in number, will indubitably prevail f. Moreover, one must understand the decision of Accursius g [to hold] when the witnesses depose to a vague and uncertain negation: for if they restricted it to certain places, times and persons, inasmuch as, being by that means narrowed, it can easily be proved h, the witnesses also who deposed to it would be no less credible than those who deposed to the affirmation i. As for example, if Antoine is accused of having murdered Pierre in Toulouse, this first day of October 1560, and some witnesses so depose, and on the contrary others say that Antoine did not do this murder, for they saw him that day at Paris: if they are equal in number, they are as credible (and the more so because they depose for innocence k) as those who would testify for the accusation and the charge l.

notes.citation: Accursius (Accurſe), the Glossa ordinaria on Digest 4.8 (De receptis: qui arbitrium receperint), l. Diem proferre, § Si plures (D. 4.8.27.3, Ulpian, on arbitrators who give differing sentences)
notes.original: Accurſe en la l. diem. P. ſi plures. D. de arbitr.
notes.gloss: The gloss's commonplace that two witnesses who affirm are to be believed before a thousand who deny, a negative not being susceptible of direct proof; the same gloss is cited at annot-038 {a} and annot-052 {a2}. The P. stands for the paragraph sign.

notes.citation: Aristotle, Metaphysics, book III as cited (the priority of affirmation to negation, and of the knowledge of what a thing is to the knowledge of what it is not; the passage is not located in book III, and the Renaissance numbering of the books differs from the modern — book number as printed)
notes.original: Ariſtote au iij. de la me taphyſique.

notes.citation: Decretals X 2.19.4 (De probationibus, c. Proposuisti) and the Doctors there
notes.original: c. propoſui cti. & illec les Docteurs, de pro.
notes.gloss: The Doctors' limitation of the rule to negatives that cannot be proved.

notes.citation: Code, title De professoribus et medicis (C. 10.53 in the modern division; the print's lib. xij places it in the twelfth book), the penultimate law (C. 10.53.10, Valentinian, Valens and Gratian: a candidate for a deceased archiater's place is admitted only when seven or more of the order judge him fit)
notes.original: l penultieme. C. de pro feſſo. & med. lib. xij.
notes.gloss: Cited for the number of doctors required to examine and approve a candidate; the Code text concerns the appointment and approval of public professors and physicians by the judgment of the order.

notes.citation: Decretals, X 2.20 (De testibus et attestationibus), c. In nostra (X 2.20.32)
notes.gloss: Where witnesses on both sides are of equal credit, the greater number prevails.

notes.citation: Accursius (Accurſe), the Gloss at § Si plures, cited above at {a}
notes.original: Accurſe au P. ſi plures. preallegué.

notes.citation: Code 8.37 (De contrahenda et committenda stipulatione), l. Optimam, toward the end (C. 8.37.14, Justinian); Decretals, X 2.23 (De praesumptionibus), c. Tertio loco (X 2.23.13)
notes.original: l. optimam. ſur la fin. C. de cont. ſtip. c. tertio loco. de præſump.
notes.gloss: A negative restricted to place, time and person is proved like an affirmative.

notes.citation: The Interpreters on Digest 45.1 (De verborum obligationibus), l. In illa (fragment not identified)
notes.original: Les Interpretes en la l. In illa. D. de verbo. oblig.

notes.citation: Decretals, X 2.19 (De probationibus), c. Ex litteris (X 2.19.3, Lucius III: where plaintiff and defendant prove equally, the defendant is absolved); Decretals, X 2.22 (De fide instrumentorum), c. Inter dilectos (X 2.22.6, Innocent III)
notes.original: c. ex literis. de probatio. c. inter de fi. inſtru.
notes.gloss: In doubt, witnesses who depose for the accused are the more favoured, reus favorabilior.

notes.citation: Accursius (Accurſe), the Gloss on Digest 43.19 (De itinere actuque privato), l. 1 (D. 43.19.1, Ulpian)
notes.original: Accurſe en la l. j. D. de Itin. actuque pri.
notes.gloss: The gloss there on proof by witnesses of equal number on either side; bearing unverified.

notes.citation: Code 4.19 (De probationibus), l. Actor (C. 4.19.23, Diocletian and Maximian); Decretals, X 1.9 (De renuntiatione), c. Super hoc (X 1.9.5); Decretals, X 2.19 (De probationibus), c. Quoniam contra (X 2.19.11, Innocent III, the Fourth Lateran Council's canon on the written record of proceedings)
notes.original: l actor C. de proba. c. ſuper hoc. de. renuncia. c. quoniam con tra. de pro,
notes.gloss: C. 4.19.23: a plaintiff who confesses he cannot prove what he asserts does not bind the defendant to prove the contrary, cum per rerum naturam factum negantis probatio nulla sit — "since by the nature of things there is no proof of one who denies a fact"; Coras's "by the nature of things" is this law's phrase.
